questions.question: The ISPE HVAC Guide aims to help readers distinguish product requirements from commercially driven, discretionary HVAC specifications. Which of the following is listed as an example of a discretionary specification?

options.A: Final HEPA filtration and cleanroom classification set according to product needs
options.B: Custom air handlers, redundant systems, all-stainless-steel ductwork, and DP controls
options.C: Critical temperature and humidity ranges determined from CPPs
options.D: Air segregation needed to prevent cross-contamination between products

questions.explanation: The Guide notes that specifications such as custom air handlers, redundant systems, all-stainless-steel air ductwork, and DP controls are often commercially driven, discretionary items. One purpose is to avoid adding facility cost without benefit (for example, over-specifying the cleanliness classification for an aseptic process). The other options are determined directly by product and process requirements.

questions.question: Why does the Guide stress that keeping operators comfortable is also part of contamination control?

options.A: Because comfortable personnel gown and wash their hands more often, reducing particle shedding to about 1,000 particles per minute, so comfort must be controlled
options.B: Because most particles shed by personnel are viable microorganisms, and their number has no real relationship to comfort or activity level, becoming more pronounced as activity increases
options.C: Because personnel are the only source of particles and equipment generates virtually none during operation, so environmental control only needs to target personnel
options.D: Because a lightly working person sheds about 100,000 particles of ≥0.3 µm per minute, and when hot and uncomfortable can shed millions and release more bacteria

questions.explanation: The Guide gives an example: a sedentary worker sheds about 100,000 particles of ≥0.3 µm per minute, and when hot and uncomfortable can shed millions and carry out more bacteria. In addition, most airborne particles are non-viable, with viable particles making up less than 1%; equipment in operation may generate even more particles, but personnel are the main source of viable contamination.

questions.question: The Guide uses the term "Grade 7". How does it relate to EU Grade B?

options.A: It is equivalent to ISO 7 (352,000/m³ at 0.5 µm) and covers in-operation limits only; Grade B has separate at-rest limits
options.B: It is another name for ISO 5; its in-operation and at-rest limits are identical to EU Grade B, and the two can be used interchangeably
options.C: It specifies only at-rest limits, whereas EU Grade B specifies only in-operation limits
options.D: It has no microbial limits, and EU Grade B sets no particle concentration limits either, specifying microbial limits only

questions.explanation: The Guide combines the EMEA term "Grade" with an ISO class number. Grade 7 corresponds to ISO 7 (in operation, 352,000/m³ at ≥0.5 µm) and looks similar to EU Grade B, but the EU Grades A to D additionally have at-rest limits.
questions.reference: ISPE HVAC Guide §1.6.6 Classified Space

questions.question: What measurable differential pressure (DP) does the Guide recommend between a Grade B or ISO 7 cleanroom and an adjacent less clean space?

options.A: About 2.5 to 5 Pa (0.01 to 0.02 inch wg); an excessive differential makes doors hard to open
options.B: About 30 to 50 Pa (0.12 to 0.2 inch wg), enough to maintain airflow direction when doors are opened
options.C: About 10 to 15 Pa (0.04 to 0.06 inch wg)
options.D: About 100 to 125 Pa (0.4 to 0.5 inch wg) to ensure complete isolation of adjacent spaces

questions.explanation: The Guide states that GMP for Grade B or ISO 7 calls for a measurable DP between the cleanroom and the adjacent less clean area, and recommends about 10 to 15 Pa between classes. Too small a value cannot be measured reliably, while too large a value creates door-operation and energy problems.
questions.reference: ISPE HVAC Guide §1.6.13; §8.3.1

questions.topic: Air change rate rules of thumb
questions.question: Designers often apply "rules of thumb" for air change rates by room class. What is the Guide's view?

options.A: They can be used directly as final design values, because the rules of thumb already cover process characteristics and no adjustment is needed
options.B: They are suitable only for concept design; air change rates should later be reduced based on process knowledge, and the rate is related to room recovery capability
options.C: The higher the air change rate the better, because raising it directly guarantees that particle concentrations are met and also shortens recovery time
options.D: Air change rate has no relationship to recovery time or room particle concentration and affects only temperature control and personnel comfort

questions.explanation: The Guide advises experienced designers to use rules of thumb only at concept design and later reduce air changes based on process knowledge. Air change rate, ventilation effectiveness, particle concentration, and the speed of recovery from in-use to at-rest conditions are interrelated; higher is not always better.
questions.reference: ISPE HVAC Guide §1.6.7; §2.2.2.4 Air Changes

questions.question: What is the first step in the HVAC design process, and why does it have the greatest impact on cost?

options.A: Selecting the AHU vendor and model, because equipment purchase price is the largest share of total construction and operating cost and must be fixed first
options.B: Writing the validation plan and test protocols, because the number and scope of validation tests directly determine overall project cost
options.C: Completing construction drawings and detailed dimensions, because drawing details directly determine duct length and material quantities and thus cost
options.D: Defining and documenting user requirements with the users and the QU, because they determine facility size and have the greatest cost impact

questions.explanation: The first step in the design process is defining user requirements, including critical HVAC performance parameters. This step has the greatest effect on the size and complexity of the facility, and therefore on construction, validation, operating, and maintenance costs, so enough time should be spent confirming it.
questions.reference: ISPE HVAC Guide §2.1.1 User Requirements

questions.question: At what points in the design process does the Guide recommend a formal design review / design qualification?

options.A: At the end of functional design and at the end of detailed design
options.B: Only once, at the PQ stage after construction is complete, to verify that final operation meets the design
options.C: Only after the purchase contract is signed, to confirm that the supplier's specifications meet user requirements
options.D: Only at the periodic annual review, as part of continual improvement and the annual quality review

questions.explanation: Using the end of functional design and the end of detailed design as examples, the Guide recommends formal design reviews to confirm that the design meets user requirements and product requirements and can be built, commissioned, operated, and maintained. Discovering design defects only after completion is the most expensive to correct.
questions.reference: ISPE HVAC Guide §2.1.4 Design Review and Qualification

questions.question: In a Grade 8 room, the final HEPA filters are leak tested once a year with no continuous monitoring, while temperature is continuously monitored by a qualified, independent SCADA system. According to the Guide's example, how should the two be managed?

options.A: Both go under quality change control and are validated, because both can affect product quality and the process
options.B: Both need only engineering change control, because HEPA and temperature control equipment are outside the AHU and not within GMP scope
options.C: The HEPA filters go under quality change control and are validated; the temperature control system can be under engineering change control after commissioning
options.D: Neither needs change control, because the HEPA filters have annual leak testing and temperature is continuously monitored

questions.explanation: The example's logic: air quality is determined directly by the final HEPA filters, and their integrity is not continuously monitored, so they must be validated and placed under quality change control. Temperature has a continuously monitoring, qualified system, so after commissioning it can remain under engineering change control.
questions.reference: ISPE HVAC Guide §2.3.3 Risk and Components (Steps 1.0–4.0)

questions.question: How does the Guide treat parameters inside the air handling unit (AHU), such as coil outlet temperature?

options.A: All are critical parameters and each must have strict acceptance criteria, to keep room conditions stable over the long term
options.B: They are usually not considered critical (supply airflow may be an exception); they are merely values that satisfy room parameters, and over-restriction should be avoided
options.C: Only temperature is critical and airflow need not be considered, because only temperature directly affects product quality
options.D: Whether they are critical depends on the AHU brand and price tier and is determined by the supplier according to its design practice

questions.explanation: The Guide states that parameters within the AHU (except possibly supply airflow) are generally not critical because they are only a means of achieving the room parameters; over-restricting parameter settings inside the AHU or ductwork should be avoided.
questions.reference: ISPE HVAC Guide §2.3.2 Impact Assessment (Notes)

questions.question: How does the HVAC risk assessment recommended by the Guide determine whether a component is critical?

options.A: By ranking components by purchase cost from highest to lowest, with the top few considered critical
options.B: By location: any component installed in the air handling plant room is considered critical
options.C: By whether the supplier offers a warranty and its length, with the vendor deciding whether the component is critical
options.D: By breaking the system into components, assessing their impact on the CPPs derived from CQAs, and judging with a challenge-question matrix

questions.explanation: The risk assessment divides the system into components and evaluates each component's impact on the CPPs (derived from CQAs). A matrix can be used, with components (such as preheat coil, fan, temperature sensor, HEPA filter) on one axis and challenge questions on the other, to decide whether each is GMP critical. Critical components require more validation and change control.
questions.reference: ISPE HVAC Guide §2.3.1; §2.3.3

questions.question: What design approach does the Guide propose to prevent airborne cross-contamination between multiple products?

options.A: Sharing one AHU and increasing the recirculation ratio, to save energy and keep pressure balance among rooms
options.B: Removing the room-to-room pressure differential requirement and relying on personnel behavior and SOPs to control cross-contamination
options.C: Rigorous air filtration, once-through air, or dedicated air handlers
options.D: Placing return air grilles only high in the ceiling, using natural convection and thermal buoyancy to carry contaminants out of the room

questions.explanation: The Guide states that the HVAC system should provide physical segregation to prevent airborne cross-contamination between products, which can be achieved with rigorous filtration, once-through air, or dedicated AHUs. Increasing the recirculation ratio would actually raise the risk of cross-contamination.
questions.reference: ISPE HVAC Guide §3.1 Introduction; §3.2.4

questions.question: An area may have solvent vapor above 25% of the LEL. How should the HVAC design handle it?

options.A: 100% once-through exhaust is recommended, because most regulations and insurers do not allow recirculation in this situation
options.B: Full recirculation is acceptable as long as a MERV 7 filter is added on the return side to remove solvent vapor
options.C: Recirculation is acceptable, but the air change rate should be reduced to a minimum to limit the amount of solvent circulating in the system
options.D: It is enough to add silencers and dampers at the return grilles; the rest of the design can be treated like an ordinary room

questions.explanation: For solvent handling, a 100% exhaust (once-through) system is recommended, possibly combined with oxygen depletion and LEL monitoring; where solvent may exceed 25% of the LEL, most regulations and insurers do not allow recirculation. For occasional small amounts of solvent, a sensor can be placed in the return duct to switch to 100% outdoor air in the event of a leak.
questions.reference: ISPE HVAC Guide §3.2.3 Hazardous Materials and their Removal

questions.question: What supply and return air arrangement does the Guide recommend for an aseptic area?

options.A: Remote HEPA filter banks in the ductwork only, with return grilles at ceiling level and a single main supply duct
options.B: Supply through ceiling terminal HEPA filters, with multiple return grilles at floor level
options.C: Low-level supply with ceiling return, so that hot air and contaminants rise naturally out of the room
options.D: A single return grille collecting all return air, to save ductwork and simplify airflow balancing

questions.explanation: The Guide recommends supplying air to the aseptic area through ceiling terminal HEPA filters (which also become part of the aseptic boundary) with multiple returns at floor level; it does not recommend relying only on remote in-duct HEPA banks, and more return grilles are better, which must not be blocked by equipment or furniture.
questions.reference: ISPE HVAC Guide §3.9.1 System Design Considerations

questions.question: What target air velocity below the filter face of a unidirectional flow hood (UFH) does the Guide recommend?

options.A: About 0.1 m/s with ±50% uniformity, to avoid air turbulence and reduce personnel discomfort
options.B: About 0.9 m/s with ±5% uniformity, to ensure stable airflow and improve particle removal efficiency
options.C: About 1.0 m/s with no uniformity requirement, as long as the overall average meets the target
options.D: About 0.45 m/s (90 ft/min) with ±20% uniformity

questions.explanation: The Guide states that the filter area of a hood should provide ISO 5 air, with a target velocity of about 90 feet per minute (0.45 m/s) and uniformity within ±20%, measured about 15 to 30 cm below the filter face.
questions.reference: ISPE HVAC Guide §3.9.1 System Design Considerations

questions.question: What pressure relationship does the Guide recommend for the gowning area of an aseptic area relative to the surrounding spaces?

options.A: Negative relative to the aseptic area and positive relative to the uncontrolled area
options.B: Positive relative to both the aseptic area and the uncontrolled area
options.C: Positive relative to the aseptic area and negative relative to the uncontrolled area
options.D: The same pressure as the aseptic area, with no differential

questions.explanation: The Guide's pressure cascade is that the room with exposed product is the most positive, with anterooms decreasing in turn to the uncontrolled area. The gowning area is supplied with HEPA-filtered air and is negative to the aseptic area and positive to the uncontrolled area; as an airlock, maintaining this relationship is what blocks contamination from moving inward.
questions.reference: ISPE HVAC Guide §3.9.1 System Design Considerations

questions.question: What common practice does the Guide describe for handling design review comments?

options.A: The user directly approves the design drawings and signs to agree, ensuring the design fully meets user needs
options.B: The designer incorporates the comments or explains why not; the user usually does not approve the design, to avoid unclear responsibility
options.C: Review comments are for reference only; the designer need not respond to each one or keep any record of how they were handled
options.D: The construction contractor decides whether to adopt the review comments and adjusts the drawings on site as conditions require

questions.explanation: A common practice is for review comments to go to the designer, who incorporates them or explains the reasons for not adopting them; the user usually does not approve the design drawings, to avoid blurring responsibility. The earlier a change is made the cheaper it is: changing the design before construction costs less than during or after construction.
questions.reference: ISPE HVAC Guide §4.1 Design Review (Design Qualification)

questions.question: What does the final, specific "quality" review (which may be called Design Qualification) mainly confirm?

options.A: Whether the purchase price is the lowest among bidders, confirming the project budget meets finance department requirements, and checking each bidder's quotation accordingly
options.B: Whether construction progress matches the original schedule and milestones, confirming on-time delivery to the user department
options.C: Whether the conditions of the HVAC system and its service areas (temperature, humidity, classification, DP, etc.) meet GMP and organizational standards
options.D: Whether the payment terms and warranty period of the purchase contract meet company finance policy, to facilitate later payment reconciliation and budget control

questions.explanation: The final quality review confirms that the HVAC system and its specified conditions (temperature, humidity, classification, DP, etc.) meet GMP and organizational standards; it may also be called DQ. ICH Q7 recommends design review, and EU regulations also state that the first element of validation for new facilities may be DQ. Commercial matters such as price, schedule, and payment terms are not the focus of this quality review.
questions.reference: ISPE HVAC Guide §4.1 Design Review (Design Qualification)

questions.question: Once the design has been accepted as suitable for its intended use, what does the Guide recommend?

options.A: Lift all document control so the design can be adjusted flexibly during construction and operation and the project can proceed faster
options.B: Review changes only before regulatory inspections and otherwise neither track them nor keep records
options.C: Let the construction contractor decide whether to change the design and simply inform the user verbally afterward
options.D: Apply formal change control to ensure the system continues to meet requirements and remains suitable for its intended use

questions.explanation: Once the design has been accepted as suitable for its intended use, formal change control should be applied to keep the system compliant. Change requests can be reviewed one by one, or at some point the system and all changes can be reviewed together as a whole.
questions.reference: ISPE HVAC Guide §4.1 Design Review (Design Qualification)

questions.question: For areas that require high system reliability (such as a vivarium), what design review approach does the Guide recommend?

options.A: A formal review such as FMEA can be used to confirm a robust design; a simplified version assessing the effect of failure on adjacent areas can also be used
options.B: No special review is needed; the HVAC design review is the same as for ordinary office space and follows the standard process
options.C: Only check actual operation during commissioning; no formal risk-based review is needed at the design stage
options.D: Review only whether the purchase price and lead time are reasonable, leaving technical details to the contractor and suppliers

questions.explanation: The Guide notes that areas with high reliability requirements can undergo a formal review, for example using Failure Modes and Effects Analysis (FMEA); a simplified version that considers the effect of system failure on adjacent areas can also be used.
questions.reference: ISPE HVAC Guide §4.1 Design Review (Design Qualification)

questions.question: Which of the following is the design review approach recommended by the Guide?

options.A: Review by the designer alone, to preserve independence of the review and shorten the overall review schedule
options.B: Review of price and lead time by the purchasing department only, with technical content left to the designer and suppliers
options.C: A multi-disciplinary team including HVAC, controls, commissioning, and regulatory SMEs, with the method agreed in advance
options.D: Review by the Quality Unit alone, with no engineering or commissioning personnel taking part in the discussion

questions.explanation: The Guide prefers review by a multi-disciplinary team including SMEs in HVAC, controls, commissioning, and regulatory matters; the review method and participants should be agreed in advance and adjusted to the type of system.
questions.reference: ISPE HVAC Guide §4.1 Design Review (Design Qualification)

questions.question: What design capacity does the Guide recommend for components of a GMP air handling unit such as coils, humidifiers, dampers, fans, motors, and filters, when designed and built?

options.A: 100%, with no margin, to save cost

questions.explanation: The Guide recommends building these components at 115% design capacity to accommodate increased demand or future expansion. This is a different number from the casing leak test condition (150% of design pressure) and the two are easily confused.
questions.reference: ISPE HVAC Guide §5.1.2 Air Handler Unit

questions.question: To reduce leakage of conditioned air, what total AHU casing leakage specification does the Guide recommend?

options.A: No more than 5% of rated airflow (at 100% design pressure) or 500 CFM, whichever is greater, and compliance with the general EN 1886 class
options.B: No more than 0.5% of rated airflow (at 150% design pressure) or 50 CFM, whichever is greater, or compliance with the most stringent EN 1886 class
options.C: No more than 0.05% of rated airflow (at design pressure), with no exceptions or greater value permitted under any circumstances
options.D: A visual check that the casing has no holes is enough; no leakage rate or leak test needs to be specified

questions.explanation: The Guide recommends that casing leakage may be specified as no more than 0.5% of rated airflow (at 150% design pressure) or 50 CFM (1.42 m³/min), whichever is greater, or compliance with the most stringent leakage class in EN 1886.
questions.reference: ISPE HVAC Guide §5.1.2.1 Cabinet Construction

questions.question: In the Guide's filtration levels, what is the function of Level II filtration and which filter is recommended?

options.A: Located downstream of Level I, it captures particles ≥0.3 µm to protect coils and fans; MERV 14 (EN F8) is recommended
options.B: Located at the outdoor air intake, it captures only large particles ≥3 µm such as insects and plant debris; a MERV 7 filter is recommended
options.C: Located at the room ceiling, it serves as final filtration for ISO 5 areas; a HEPA filter is recommended, with a pre-filter added at the intake as support
options.D: Located at the return air grille, it collects room dust and fibers; a 30% dust-stop filter is recommended

questions.explanation: Level I (MERV 7, EN G4) is a low-cost pre-filter that captures large particles ≥3 µm from outdoor air and extends the life of Level II. Level II sits downstream of it, captures smaller particles (≥0.3 µm) to protect the coils and fans, and MERV 14 (EN F8) is recommended. Only the final (terminal) filtration uses HEPA.
questions.reference: ISPE HVAC Guide §5.2.5.2 Level II Filtration

questions.question: How does the Guide recommend deciding when to replace the filter stages in an AHU?

options.A: Strictly on a fixed schedule, for example replacing all filters every six months regardless of DP or usage
options.B: Wait until airflow drops noticeably or operators complain about poor air conditioning, then schedule replacement
options.C: Fit a DP gauge on each stage and replace when the optimum DP limit is reached; time alone may lead to premature or late replacement
options.D: Replace all filters together only during the annual validation, with no DP checks or filter condition monitoring at other times

questions.explanation: The Guide recommends a DP gauge (Magnehelic or manometer) on every filter bank to monitor pressure drop as loading increases, with replacement based on a pre-established optimum DP limit; replacing on time alone can waste filters or replace them too late.
questions.reference: ISPE HVAC Guide §5.2.2 Filter Installations

questions.question: For fan installation and startup, what does the Guide recommend for adjusting drive belt tension?

options.A: Adjust to the correct tension before startup and re-adjust the tension after 24 hours of operation
options.B: Leave it as set at the factory to avoid affecting the warranty, with no further checks of belt wear
options.C: Loosen the belt before startup and tighten it after one week of operation
options.D: Re-adjust only after one year of operation

questions.explanation: Belts should be adjusted to the correct tension before startup and re-adjusted after 24 hours of operation. In addition, the fan and motor should be laser-aligned on site, and if a variable frequency drive (VFD) is present, start at low speed and raise it slowly while watching for noise, vibration, and bearing overheating.
questions.reference: ISPE HVAC Guide §5.3.3 Fans

questions.question: By when does the Guide recommend that the life cycle of HVAC project documents be defined, at the latest?

options.A: During concept design, and no later than functional (schematic) design
options.B: After construction is complete, compiled from actual installation results and as-built site conditions
options.C: After validation is complete, filling in the documents based on the validation report and conclusions
options.D: One month before a customer audit, so that documents and records needed for the audit are prepared in time

questions.explanation: The Guide recommends defining the document life cycle at concept design and no later than Functional/Schematic design, to reduce ambiguity and avoid loss of data, and to decide which documents go into the Engineering Turnover Package (ETOP).
questions.reference: ISPE HVAC Guide §6.2.1 Planning Life Cycle

questions.question: After construction, the actual layout differs from the original design drawings. According to the Guide, how should the drawings be handled?

options.A: Leave the original design drawings unchanged and explain the differences between actual and design verbally in the maintenance manual, with maintenance staff adding explanatory material later
options.B: Delete the original drawings and use site photographs and construction records as the only drawing basis
options.C: Update them at the next system modification, and in the meantime just annotate the differences by hand on the drawings
options.D: Update them to as-built to match the final configuration, which is especially important for drawings of systems that monitor or control critical parameters

questions.explanation: The Guide states that plans, details, and drawings should be updated to as-built during or after construction. This is vital for maintenance and especially important for systems that monitor and control critical parameters.
questions.reference: ISPE HVAC Guide §6.2.2 Typical Steps in the Document Life Cycle

questions.question: Why do "Critical Master Documents" require special control?

options.A: Because they are used only internally by maintenance staff and are not provided externally, so access must be restricted
options.B: Because once approved they never need to be updated or revised, so they must be locked and kept long term
options.C: Because they provide the HVAC information needed for the CMC section of regulatory filings and are subject to regulatory review
options.D: Because they are only design-stage drafts that have not yet become formal documents and must be kept from circulating

questions.explanation: Critical Master Documents define the critical attributes of the HVAC system, serve as content for CMC filings, and are subject to regulatory review, so they must be maintained as GMP records.
questions.reference: ISPE HVAC Guide §6.5.2 Critical Master Documents

questions.question: What is the purpose of using a Traceability Matrix in document management?

options.A: Solely to list contact details of suppliers and contractors, contract numbers, and delivery dates for each phase
options.B: To track the progression of documents and concepts from design through construction and validation to process validation, showing that the HVAC is fit for service
options.C: To replace all commissioning and validation documents so the project need not produce separate test protocols and reports
options.D: Solely to calculate the project construction budget and payment progress for each phase, with no tracking of documents or requirements, signed off monthly by the project manager

questions.explanation: The Traceability Matrix records the plan and progress of documents and concepts from design through construction and validation to process validation, is used to plan and update the document life cycle, and demonstrates that the HVAC is fit for service.
questions.reference: ISPE HVAC Guide §6.2.1 Planning Life Cycle

questions.question: Which of the following is a document typically produced during commissioning and qualification (C&Q) or process validation?

options.A: A concept-stage room conditions table and preliminary area layout, used to define the scope of user requirements
options.B: Tender documents and supplier qualification records, used to select the design and construction contractors
options.C: Preliminary construction drawings and integrated multi-discipline drawings, used to coordinate duct and pipe routing
options.D: Airflow visualization records for Grade 5 (EU Grade A) or localized protection zones under in-use conditions

questions.explanation: The Guide lists the documents typically produced during C&Q, including airflow visualization for Grade 5 (Grade A) or localized protection zones. A room conditions table is an early conceptual document and is not a C&Q output.
questions.reference: ISPE HVAC Guide §6.5.1 Commissioning and Qualification Documents

questions.topic: Air velocity for comfort vs product protection
questions.question: What air velocities does Appendix 1 mention for office environment design versus product protection needs?

options.A: About 1 m/s for offices and about 0.1 m/s for product protection, because product protection needs lower airflow to avoid turbulence, since higher velocity makes particles settle and increases contamination
options.B: Both about 0.1 m/s, with no difference by use, because air velocity has nothing to do with particle capture
options.C: About 0.1 m/s for offices; to capture particles, product protection can be as high as about 1 m/s (200 ft/min)
options.D: Both must exceed 5 m/s to achieve effective dilution and remove airborne particles

questions.explanation: The Guide notes that gentle airflow is usually perceived as better, and a typical office design value is 0.1 m/s (0.3 ft/s); to protect product and capture particles, higher velocities are usually needed, up to about 1 m/s (200 ft/min).
questions.reference: ISPE HVAC Guide Appendix 1 §7.2.1.2 Air Movement

questions.question: For general, non-contaminated work spaces, approximately how much fresh air per person does ASHRAE 62 recommend?

options.A: About 1 to 2 CFM (1.7 to 3.4 m³/h) per person
options.B: About 15 to 20 CFM (24 to 32 m³/h) per person
options.C: About 150 to 200 CFM (240 to 320 m³/h) per person
options.D: About 1,500 CFM (approximately 2,550 m³/h) per person

questions.explanation: Fresh air is used to dilute carbon dioxide, odors, and other environmental contaminants. Unless a complex ASHRAE analysis is performed, ASHRAE 62 recommends 15 to 20 CFM (24 to 32 m³/h) per person for non-contaminated work spaces, and local building codes may require different values.
questions.reference: ISPE HVAC Guide Appendix 1 §7.2.1.3 Air Quality

questions.question: Appendix 1 discusses the effect of ambient humidity on product. Which statement is correct?

options.A: High humidity can increase the growth rate of microorganisms and mold on surfaces
options.B: Humidity affects only personnel comfort and has nothing to do with microorganisms
options.C: The higher the humidity, the fewer the particles, so it benefits contamination control
options.D: No matter how large the difference between indoor and outdoor conditions, condensation is never a problem

questions.explanation: The Guide states that high humidity increases microbial and mold growth on surfaces; in addition, when the difference between indoor and outdoor conditions is large and building envelope integrity is inadequate, condensation can form in interstitial spaces, leading to microbial contamination and material deterioration.
questions.reference: ISPE HVAC Guide Appendix 1 §7.2.2 Product and Process Considerations

questions.question: When a product is sensitive to environmental conditions and this is considered critical, where are these product environmental requirements usually recorded?

options.A: Only on the air handler nameplate
options.B: Only in the maintenance staff's notes
options.C: Only in the vendor's sales brochure
options.D: The New Drug Application (NDA)

questions.explanation: Appendix 1 states that when considered critical, a product's environmental requirements are usually listed in the NDA, and new drug development data may also be available. The effect of out-of-range conditions depends on the duration of exposure.
questions.reference: ISPE HVAC Guide Appendix 1 §7.2.2 Product and Process Considerations

questions.question: In areas requiring heavier over-garments or more strenuous work, how should room conditions be set compared with an office area?

options.A: Hotter and more humid, so personnel sweat and shed fewer particles
options.B: Exactly the same as the office area, so personnel keep sweating and shedding heat inside their cleanroom garments
options.C: Cooler and drier, to avoid discomfort for personnel wearing cleanroom garments
options.D: Only differential pressure needs to be controlled; temperature and humidity are not important

questions.explanation: The Guide states that general non-production areas should fall within the comfort zone; if gowning is heavier or work is more vigorous, room conditions should be cooler and less humid than in an office. Uncomfortable personnel shed more particles.
questions.reference: ISPE HVAC Guide Appendix 1 §7.2.1.1 Temperature and Humidity

questions.question: In an AHU using a large amount of outdoor air in a cold climate, where is the preheat coil usually placed, and why?

options.A: Upstream of the cooling coil, to protect the cooling coil from freezing
options.B: Downstream of the final HEPA filter, to compensate for the HEPA pressure drop
options.C: At the fan outlet, to reduce fan noise
options.D: In the room, to adjust local temperature

questions.explanation: Systems with once-through air or a large amount of cold outdoor air can use a preheat coil to treat the intake or mixed air. It is placed upstream of the cooling coil to prevent freezing, and may also be placed upstream of the filters to melt frost and snow.
questions.reference: ISPE HVAC Guide Appendix 2 §8.1.7.1 Preheat Coil

questions.question: Systems that dehumidify by overcooling usually add a reheat coil. What is its purpose?

options.A: To increase the humidity of air entering the AHU so the humidifier can run at lower energy consumption and remain stable
options.B: To replace the function of the cooling coil, saving equipment count and installation cost and simplifying the system configuration
options.C: To heat the air leaving the cooling coil, avoiding overcooling and lowering RH to prevent condensation
options.D: To filter particles from the air, protecting the downstream fan, ductwork, and final HEPA filter

questions.explanation: Systems that dehumidify by overcooling (rather than by desiccant dehumidification) use a reheat coil to warm the air leaving the cooling coil, avoiding an overcooled room and lowering the RH of the AHU discharge air to prevent condensation in the ductwork.
questions.reference: ISPE HVAC Guide Appendix 2 §8.1.7.2 Reheat Coil

questions.question: For steam used in humidification, what is the Guide's view on using clean steam (generated from purified water or WFI)?

options.A: Clean steam made from WFI is mandatory, with dedicated steam filtration and condensing equipment added
options.B: Only direct spraying of tap water may be used
options.C: Boiler steam containing volatile additives must be used
options.D: It is generally considered wasteful, because steam generated in copper, brass, or stainless steel systems is already adequate for the cleanliness required in classified spaces

questions.explanation: The Appendix states that using clean steam generated from USP purified water or WFI for humidification is considered wasteful, because steam generated without volatile additives in copper, brass, or stainless steel systems is sufficient for classified spaces.
questions.reference: ISPE HVAC Guide Appendix 2 §8.1.9 Humidifier

questions.question: What does Appendix 2 recommend for the locations of supply and return air in classified spaces?

options.A: Both supply and return at ceiling level, to shorten duct paths and reduce system pressure drop
options.B: Supply at ceiling level, with return or exhaust near the floor (low-wall returns about 30 cm above the floor)
options.C: Supply at floor level and return at ceiling level, so air carries particles away from bottom to top
options.D: As long as total airflow is sufficient, the locations of supply and return do not matter and do not affect the airflow pattern

questions.explanation: GMP spaces and cleanrooms need a more rigorous airflow arrangement: supply at ceiling height, return and general exhaust near the floor, and process exhaust as close to the source as possible; low-wall returns keep contaminants below the work surface, at about 12 inches (30 cm) above the floor.
questions.reference: ISPE HVAC Guide Appendix 2 §8.4.1.3 Room Air Supply Distribution Options

questions.question: Ethanol vapor from an open granulator is a hazardous material that must be controlled. Of the three approaches in Appendix 2, which should be used?

options.A: Capture at the source, such as a high-velocity LEV capture hood
options.B: Release and dilution, diluting with room air
options.C: Only increasing the room air change rate, and adding air curtains and high-speed supply fans along the whole line
options.D: Only an air curtain at the doorway

questions.explanation: Release and dilution suits materials that are mildly unpleasant but harmless; materials that are hazardous, endanger health or safety, or are flammable should be captured at the source with LEV (for example a capture hood for ethanol vapor from an open granulator); extremely hazardous materials call for containment and exhaust (such as a glove box).
questions.reference: ISPE HVAC Guide Appendix 2 §8.4.2 Extract (Exhaust/Return) Strategies

questions.question: On a psychrometric chart, in what direction are the dry-bulb temperature and dew-point temperature lines drawn?

options.A: Both are horizontal lines, and neither changes with dry-bulb temperature or moisture content; they represent pressure only
options.B: Dry-bulb temperature is a horizontal line and dew point is a vertical line
options.C: Both are vertical lines
options.D: Dry-bulb temperature is a vertical line and dew-point temperature is a horizontal line

questions.explanation: Dry-bulb temperature is shown as vertical lines, increasing from left to right; dew-point temperature is shown as horizontal lines that intersect the saturation curve (the left boundary of the chart). Wet-bulb and enthalpy lines are diagonals running from upper left to lower right.
questions.reference: ISPE HVAC Guide Appendix 3 §9.2 Dry-Bulb Temperature; §9.4 Dew-Point Temperature

questions.question: Which description of relative humidity (RH) in Appendix 3 is correct?

options.A: The absolute weight of water vapor in the air, independent of temperature, in kg of water vapor per m³ of air
options.B: The ratio of the amount of water vapor to the maximum the air can hold at the same temperature and pressure; the hotter the air, the more it can hold
options.C: The ratio of the mass of dry air to the mass of water vapor, in kg/kg, unrelated to air temperature
options.D: The dew-point temperature of the air expressed as a percentage, where a higher value means less moisture in the air

questions.explanation: RH is the percentage relative to the maximum amount of water vapor at the same temperature and pressure; the higher the temperature, the more moisture the air can hold. The quantity that is independent of temperature and expressed as a mass ratio is the humidity ratio.
questions.reference: ISPE HVAC Guide Appendix 3 §9.5 Relative Humidity

questions.question: What is characteristic of the humidity ratio?

options.A: It varies with air temperature and is expressed as a percentage, so it is unsuitable for load calculations
options.B: It applies only to air below 0°C, used to estimate the energy needed for coil frosting and defrosting
options.C: It reflects the actual amount of water in the air, independent of temperature, in units such as kg of water vapor per kg of dry air
options.D: It is unrelated to water vapor pressure and depends only on the total air pressure, in Pa or inch wg

questions.explanation: The humidity ratio is the ratio of the weight of water vapor to the weight of dry air; it represents the actual water content and is not affected by temperature. Water vapor pressure also rises as specific humidity increases, so the two are related.
questions.reference: ISPE HVAC Guide Appendix 3 §9.9 Humidity Ratio or Specific Humidity

questions.question: Why do calculations need to be adjusted when designing HVAC at locations above 2,000 ft (about 600 m)?

options.A: The air is thinner, so a larger volume must be moved to achieve the same mass flow, and specific volume and density must be corrected
options.B: The air is denser, so airflow must be reduced to maintain the same mass flow, and specific volume and density must be corrected
options.C: Thermometers read with a bias at high altitude, so all temperature readings must be recalibrated before use
options.D: Wet-bulb temperature cannot be measured at high altitude, so dew-point sensors must replace wet-bulb calculations

questions.explanation: The higher the altitude, the thinner the air, and a larger volume must be moved to deliver the air mass required by the design, so above 2,000 ft (600 m) the specific volume and density calculations should be adjusted.
questions.reference: ISPE HVAC Guide Appendix 3 §9.8 Specific Volume

questions.question: What does enthalpy represent in HVAC calculations?

options.A: Only dry (sensible) heat, excluding the energy carried by moisture, used to calculate cooling load
options.B: Only the partial pressure of water vapor, independent of air temperature and dry heat, in Pa or kPa
options.C: The volume occupied by a unit mass of air, in m³/kg of dry air, used to convert airflow
options.D: Latent heat (moisture) plus sensible heat, with the difference used to quantify the total heat added or removed in a process

questions.explanation: Enthalpy measures both latent heat (moisture) and sensible heat (dry heat), and the enthalpy difference quantifies the total thermal energy added or removed in an HVAC process. The quantity representing only dry heat is sensible heat, and the volume occupied is the specific volume.
questions.reference: ISPE HVAC Guide Appendix 3 §9.7 Specific Enthalpy

questions.question: What are the two primary principles of quality risk management as defined by ICH Q9?

options.A: Risk must be completely eliminated, and all risks are handled with the same level of formality and documentation detail
options.B: Risk evaluation is based on scientific knowledge and linked to patient protection; effort, formality, and documentation are commensurate with the level of risk
options.C: Risk is assessed only by the supplier, and the results need not be recorded or made available for user review
options.D: Risk is assessed only after a deviation occurs, by QA alone, with no involvement of other departments

questions.explanation: The two ICH Q9 principles: the evaluation of the risk to quality should be based on scientific knowledge and ultimately linked to the protection of the patient; and the level of effort, formality, and documentation of the quality risk management process should be commensurate with the level of risk.
questions.reference: ISPE HVAC Guide Appendix 4 §10.1 ICH Q9 Quality Risk Management Approach

questions.question: How does Appendix 4 define "risk"?

options.A: The combination of the probability of occurrence of harm and the severity of that harm
options.B: Only the severity of harm, which must additionally be multiplied by a regulatory standard value to be calculated
options.C: Only the probability of occurrence of harm
options.D: Only the standard required by regulations

questions.explanation: Risk is the combination of the probability of occurrence of harm and the severity of that harm; severity alone is only a measure of the possible consequences of a hazard. The ability to detect harm should also be considered in risk analysis.
questions.reference: ISPE HVAC Guide Appendix 4 §10.1 ICH Q9 Quality Risk Management Approach

questions.question: What is Appendix 4's view on the goal of risk management?

options.A: Reduce risk to zero, which is required to meet regulations and obtain approval
options.B: Only record the risk; no action to reduce risk is needed
options.C: Reduce it to an acceptable level; completely eliminating risk is neither practical nor necessary
options.D: Manage only risks that have already occurred, with no need to assess potential risks

questions.explanation: Risk management should bring risk down to an acceptable level, and the Guide states explicitly that completely eliminating risk is neither practical nor necessary; the decision framework should be incorporated into the quality management system to maintain consistency.
questions.reference: ISPE HVAC Guide Appendix 4 (introduction to §10, Science-Based Quality Risk Management)

questions.question: In a risk assessment, which step is comparing the analyzed risk against established risk criteria?

options.A: Risk identification
options.B: Risk analysis
options.C: Risk communication
options.D: Risk evaluation

questions.explanation: Risk identification uses information to find hazards; risk analysis estimates risk by linking the likelihood of occurrence to severity (also considering detectability); risk evaluation compares the identified and analyzed risk against established risk criteria.
questions.reference: ISPE HVAC Guide Appendix 4 §10.4 Risk Assessment

questions.question: Which of the following is an example of a maintenance-related hazard identification listed in Appendix 4?

options.A: A new building using too many rare metals
options.B: Use of an inappropriate spare part contaminating the product
options.C: Operators having an untidy appearance
options.D: Inconsistent line thickness on construction drawings

questions.explanation: The Appendix lists maintenance-related risk examples, including product contamination caused by maintenance work (such as using an inappropriate spare part), facility or equipment design that is unfavorable to proper maintenance, and maintenance that takes critical equipment out of service without production being aware.
questions.reference: ISPE HVAC Guide Appendix 4 §10.4 Risk Assessment

questions.question: In the Appendix's risk example, a supply air CV box failure causes room airflow imbalance and its detection capability is rated high. What is the reason?

options.A: Because operators manually measure airflow and record it every hour, so an airflow imbalance is found in time
options.B: Because the CV box has a built-in automatic calibration function that corrects deviations itself without personnel intervention
options.C: A DP alarm can detect changes in room differential pressure, and daily in-operation particle monitoring can detect changes in particles
options.D: Because after the failure the air handler stops automatically, so room airflow ceases immediately and triggers an alarm

questions.explanation: The example notes that a change in airflow changes the room particle count and differential pressure, with a moderate impact; the DP alarm (provided there is no DP control in the room that masks the problem) and daily in-operation particle monitoring can detect the change, so detection capability is high.
questions.reference: ISPE HVAC Guide Appendix 5 §11.1.1 Example One – Classified Space

questions.question: If the fan or HEPA filter of a unidirectional flow hood fails, the risk to product exposed under the hood is high. What detection method does the example recommend?

options.A: Rely only on a motor current switch to judge whether the fan is running, with the detector mounted directly above critical locations inside the hood
options.B: Rely only on the operator visually judging during work whether airflow and smoke under the hood are normal, with no separate sensor, and personnel deciding to stop work themselves if hood velocity drops
options.C: Confirm the fan and HEPA status only at the annual inspection, with no continuous monitoring at other times
options.D: Monitor with an airflow switch (not a motor current switch) or a hot-wire anemometer at the filter face, but not placed in the airflow path leading to critical locations

questions.explanation: In the example, a fan failure or HEPA failure creates a high risk of product exposure and operators may not notice it. The recommendation is to monitor with an airflow switch (not a motor current switch) or a filter-face hot-wire anemometer, with the sensor not placed in the airflow path to the critical location, and to add a velocity check during HEPA scan testing.
questions.reference: ISPE HVAC Guide Appendix 5 §11.1.2 Example Two – Classified Space

questions.question: A room pressure control damper operates improperly, causing pressure reversal. What mitigation does the example recommend?

options.A: Periodically calibrate and challenge the DP monitoring, and ignore the transient DP changes from door openings (confirming an acceptable delay)
options.B: Remove all DP monitoring to avoid nuisance alarms, and rely on personnel to visually confirm daily instead
options.C: Set the pressure alarm permanently to silent so it does not disturb work, enabling it only during audits
options.D: Shut down immediately on any DP change, including momentary changes caused by door openings, to ensure product safety

questions.explanation: The example recommends periodic calibration and challenge of DP monitoring, and confirming an acceptable time delay so that transient DP changes from door openings are ignored. Pressure control is harder to maintain in large systems, and pressure reversal can carry contamination from room to room, a high risk to product.
questions.reference: ISPE HVAC Guide Appendix 5 §11.1.3 Example Three – Pressure Controlled Space

questions.question: For a campaigned multi-product OSD facility sharing one AHU, what are the main risk and the measure recommended by the example?

options.A: The main risk is excessive temperature affecting equipment operation; the recommendation is to enlarge cooling coil capacity and increase supply airflow
options.B: The main risk is cross-contamination from HVAC backflow or duct residue; process in pressurized containment equipment and do not recirculate the exhaust
options.C: The main risk is excessive noise affecting operators; the recommendation is to add silencers and more sound insulation, and increase duct cleaning frequency and downtime
options.D: The main risk is high energy cost increasing operating expense; the recommendation is to reduce airflow and shorten operating hours

questions.explanation: The example's risk is cross-contamination from HVAC backflow, from residues of a previous product left in ductwork, or from different products running in other rooms. Measures include placing the process in an enclosure or containment equipment, not recirculating the process exhaust from the isolator, and capturing material in the ductwork with terminal HEPA filters.
questions.reference: ISPE HVAC Guide Appendix 5 §11.1.4 Example Four – Multi-Product Campaigned OSD Facility with One AHU

questions.question: How does the ISPE Baseline Guide on Commissioning and Qualification recommend arranging commissioning and qualification tests for HVAC?

options.A: Complete qualification during commissioning, without repeating the commissioning tests
options.B: Perform every test twice, once at the commissioning stage and once at the qualification stage, to ensure correctness and to allow cross-comparison of results from the two stages
options.C: Perform only qualification, omitting all tests and records in the commissioning stage
options.D: Test only at the process validation stage, with no separate testing at the commissioning and qualification stages

questions.explanation: The Appendix notes that the C&Q Guide recommends qualifying at the time of commissioning rather than repeating commissioning tests for qualification. ISO 14644-3 provides the procedures for testing cleanroom performance, such as particle count classification.
questions.reference: ISPE HVAC Guide Appendix 7 – ISO 14644-3 – A Qualification Document

questions.question: What commonly used method does Appendix 9 mention for evaluating the economics of different HVAC design options?

options.A: Compare only the lowest initial purchase price of each option, ignoring service life and maintenance cost
options.B: Compare only the power consumption of each option during operation, ignoring initial investment and maintenance expense
options.C: Compare only the format and payment terms of vendor quotations, ignoring the equipment life cycle
options.D: Net present value (NPV) or rate of return

questions.explanation: The Guide states that net present value or rate of return is commonly used to evaluate design options, but these concepts are often unfamiliar to engineers focused on the most robust design; cost models should also include the overall impact of production cost, downtime, and product loss.
questions.reference: ISPE HVAC Guide Appendix 9 §15.1 HVAC System Economics

questions.question: What is the effect on an HVAC system of specifying closer control tolerances?

options.A: It always makes the system more robust and, because control is more precise, usually reduces equipment capacity and operating cost
options.B: It affects only appearance and the operating interface, not equipment capacity, and does not change installation or operating cost
options.C: It is not necessarily more robust; a system with larger capacity and faster response is needed and costs more, while a wider range can reduce cost
options.D: It reduces the required equipment capacity, because with more precise control the air handling load also decreases

questions.explanation: The Appendix notes that wider operating ranges can reduce system cost, while closer tolerances do not necessarily provide a "better" system; to maintain tight tolerances, a facility may need to be designed with larger capacity and faster response, increasing cost.
questions.reference: ISPE HVAC Guide Appendix 9 §15.1.1.4 Defining User Requirements

questions.question: What is Appendix 9's warning about over-specification?

options.A: The higher the specification the safer, so cost need not be considered in design and the highest specification should simply be adopted
options.B: Over-specifying classification, air change rates, and DP increases life cycle cost without adding value for the product
options.C: Over-specification only increases noise and vibration and has no effect on initial cost or life cycle energy consumption
options.D: Over-specification does not affect validation scope, only appearance and equipment layout, needs no special review, and reduces the number of validation tests as a result

questions.explanation: The Guide explicitly advises against over-specifying area classification, air change rates, and DP, since doing so leads to higher life cycle cost without adding value for the product.
questions.reference: ISPE HVAC Guide Appendix 9 §15.1.1.4 Defining User Requirements

questions.question: Regarding the energy efficiency of fan drives, which statement from Appendix 9 is correct?

options.A: Traditional V-belts can lose up to about 7% efficiency due to wear and improper tension; use direct-drive fans where feasible
options.B: V-belts have the highest efficiency and are easy to maintain, so they should be preferred over direct-drive fans
options.C: Belt type and tension condition do not affect efficiency, all belt types have roughly the same energy loss, and the same efficiency is maintained at any speed
options.D: Direct-drive fans have lower efficiency than traditional V-belt drive fans because they lack speed variability

questions.explanation: Traditional V-belts can lose up to 7% efficiency through slip, and direct drive greatly reduces this; synchronous belts or flat belts are about 2% more efficient than V-belts, generate less heat, and last longer.
questions.reference: ISPE HVAC Guide Appendix 9 §15.1.2.3 Energy Costs and Trends (Drive Belts)

questions.question: When does the Guide consider duplication/redundancy of systems or equipment justified?

options.A: Whenever the budget allows, to improve overall system availability and operating stability
options.B: Only for visual symmetry and attractive equipment layout, unrelated to system reliability and risk reduction
options.C: When both the cost and the likelihood of failure are high; but redesigning the system or process to reduce the risk may be better
options.D: Only during the first year of operation, with redundancy gradually removed afterward to reduce maintenance cost

questions.explanation: The Appendix notes that where both the cost and the likelihood of failure are high, duplicating equipment may be worthwhile; however, redesigning the system or process to reduce risk is often the better choice, because redundancy makes design, startup, and maintenance more complex.
questions.reference: ISPE HVAC Guide Appendix 9 §15.1.1.2 Redundancy

questions.question: Appendix 10 describes FDA medical device classes. Which class has the strictest regulation?

options.A: Class I, because it is the most numerous and widest in scope and requires the strictest premarket review
options.B: Class III, typically devices that support or sustain life and for which general and special controls are insufficient
options.C: Class II, because it requires special controls and premarket notification, giving the highest level of regulation
options.D: All three classes are regulated equally and differ only in name according to device name and use

questions.explanation: Class I has the least regulation (general controls, such as elastic bandages and examination gloves); Class II requires special controls; Class III is the strictest, for devices where information is insufficient to assure safety and effectiveness through general or special controls alone, typically those that support or sustain life. Many Class I and II devices need only comfort HVAC or CNC.
questions.reference: ISPE HVAC Guide Appendix 10 §16.1 Introduction

questions.topic: Crack velocity at a given DP
questions.question: Using a simplified formula, Appendix 11 estimates the air velocity through gaps such as door cracks for a DP of 0.05 inch wg (12.5 Pa) between two rooms. What is it approximately?

options.A: About 89 ft/min
options.B: About 8,900 ft/min
options.C: About 100 ft/min
options.D: About 890 ft/min

questions.explanation: In the Appendix's example, a velocity pressure of 0.05 inch wg (12.5 Pa) corresponds to an air velocity of about 890 ft/min. The formula ignores entrance losses and pressure recovery, so the calculated velocity is greater than what is actually needed to produce that differential.
questions.reference: ISPE HVAC Guide Appendix 11 §17.1.1 Room DP

questions.question: According to the glossary, what is the difference between a Direct Impact System and an Indirect Impact System?

options.A: The design and validation requirements of the two are identical and only the names differ, with the difference being the system category and budget, and the Indirect system additionally requiring full PQ and process validation
options.B: Indirect systems need stricter validation than Direct systems, because their impact covers the whole plant
options.C: A Direct system is expected to directly affect product quality and requires qualification in addition to GEP; an Indirect system is usually handled by GEP alone
options.D: A Direct system needs only to be designed to GEP, with no review, verification, or qualification activities

questions.explanation: A Direct Impact System is expected to have a direct impact on product quality and, in addition to GEP, includes validation with enhanced review, control, and testing. An Indirect Impact System is not expected to have a direct impact on product quality but usually supports Direct systems, and is designed and commissioned to GEP only.
questions.reference: ISPE HVAC Guide Appendix 13 §19.3 Definitions: Direct Impact System / Indirect Impact System

questions.question: What does the glossary say about "Grade", and how do EU GMP Grades A to D differ from ISO 14644-1?

options.A: EU Grades A to D additionally have at-rest particle limits, whereas the ISO 14644-1 numbers represent in-operation upper limits only
options.B: EU Grades A to D regulate only the at-rest state and do not regulate in-operation particle concentration or microbial limits
options.C: The two are identical, with no difference in at-rest or in-operation particle limits, and can be substituted for each other
options.D: ISO 14644-1 regulates at-rest limits in addition, whereas EU GMP regulates only in-operation upper limits

questions.explanation: The glossary states that Grade refers to the in-operation upper limit of particle counts (the number determined by ISO 14644-1), and European GMP Grades A to D additionally have at-rest limits, so the requirements on HVAC design are stricter.
questions.reference: ISPE HVAC Guide Appendix 13 §19.3 Definitions: Grade

questions.question: What is a Design Target in the glossary, and can it be used for system validation?

options.A: It is equivalent to an acceptance criterion and should be used directly for system validation as the basis for pass or fail
options.B: It is merely a vendor's sales target, unrelated to the actual design and does not appear in design documents
options.C: It is an observed value from actual operation and can be used as the basis for setting alert and action limits
options.D: A design value more conservative than the acceptance criterion; as an ideal value, it should not be used for system validation

questions.explanation: A Design Target is a value more conservative than the acceptance criterion of a critical parameter, allowing the designer to ensure the system can meet the acceptance criterion; it is an "ideal" value that may not be achievable in practice, so it should not be used for system validation. The normal operating range is the value actually observed in operation.
questions.reference: ISPE HVAC Guide Appendix 13 §19.3 Definitions: Design Target
